description: Specializing in advanced data extraction and process optimization. My goal is to apply commercial data engineering solutions to solve the MODIS/VIIRS harmonization challenge, transforming raw, distributed satellite data into a fast, scalable, and user-friendly interface.
summary: ThermalETL turns NASA FIRMS hotspot data from two satellites, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), into one consistent fire history that anyone can understand. The two sensors detect fires very differently, so simply joining them makes fire activity seem to explode in 2012 and breaks long-term trends. We aggregate all detections into H3 hexagons and compute a VIIRS-to-MODIS coefficient for every hexagon and every calendar month, falling back to a wider area when data is thin. This rescales the 2000–2012 MODIS record onto the VIIRS scale. On a held-out year, this local coefficient reduced prediction error by 25.4% compared with a single regional ratio. In our web app, users draw an area or enter coordinates, pick a date range, and see a clear fire calendar: the main fire seasons, the most active years, and how the current period compares with the historical median, explained in plain language with colour-blind-safe scales. Results can be exported as CSV. The pipeline is free, open source, and updates automatically through GitHub Actions. It helps firefighters, municipalities, foresters and citizens plan around real local fire patterns without needing GIS skills or an AI chatbot.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ThermalETL builds one consistent 2000–today fire-activity record from NASA FIRMS hotspots of MODIS (Terra/Aqua, 1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS S-NPP (375 m, since 2012), and presents it as an easy fire calendar for any area.

HOW IT WORKS

1. GitHub Actions download FIRMS data with the FIRMS API, filter by confidence and store it as Parquet.

2. Detections are aggregated into Uber H3 hexagons (resolution 5) as monthly counts per sensor.

3. For each hexagon and calendar month we compute k = VIIRS / MODIS over the overlap years (2012+). When local support is too small, we fall back to the parent hexagon, a wider area, and finally the region.

4. The harmonized series uses VIIRS where available and MODIS × k before 2012.

5. For each area we compute the monthly median and 90th percentile across years, then flag above-normal months, the most active years and the critical fire season.

Validation on a held-out year (2023, 4,913 hexagon-months in Poland): mean absolute error 5.44 with per-hex k vs 7.28 with one regional ratio, a 25.4% improvement.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Users draw an area or type coordinates, choose dates and immediately see when fires usually happen, which years were exceptional and whether the current period is above the historical median, in plain language. CSV export supports further analysis. It is meant for firefighters and civil protection, municipalities, foresters, insurers, researchers and citizens who need local fire patterns without GIS skills.

TOOLS

Python, DuckDB, H3, Parquet, pytest; TypeScript, Next.js, Tailwind, MapLibre GL, deck.gl, h3-js; GitHub Actions; Vercel; OpenFreeMap basemap. AI coding assistant (Cursor) used for implementation.

CREATIVITY

Instead of one correction factor per region, we harmonize locally per hexagon and month, because the difference between sensors depends on landscape and season. The result is shown as a calendar, not a complex GIS tool.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Accessibility (colour-blind-safe scales, keyboard use), transparency (each hexagon shows its coefficient, data support and fallback level), zero-cost open-source infrastructure with automatic updates, and honest limitations: hotspots are not burned area, detections depend on clouds and overpasses, and MODIS is nearing retirement, so VIIRS is the long-term reference scale. Demo region: Poland; the pipeline is region-agnostic.
dataRefs: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra & Aqua) standard product, confidence ≥ 30.
